common_name: Jubilee Hens and Chicks (Silvery Rose Sempervivum)

planting.note: Nestle offsets onto the surface of lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in spring or fall, since this older English selection resents soggy ground far more than cold.

directions: 'Jubilee' forms neat, symmetrical rosettes in a soft silvery-rose wash that intensifies toward the tips, giving a cleaner, more uniform color than many older tectorum-type hybrids. Full sun and mineral, fast-draining soil bring out the strongest color and keep the rosettes compact rather than open and lax. Like all sempervivums, individual rosettes flower once on a stout stalk and then die, but the surrounding offsets multiply readily and quickly close any gap. It is a reliable, long-cultivated variety for trough gardens, wall crevices, and rock garden edging where winter wet can be kept to a minimum.

common_name: Rubies Edge Hens and Chicks (Green Rosette with Ruby Margin)

planting.note: Set offsets on the surface of lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun, which is essential for the ruby leaf margins to color fully.

directions: 'Rubies Edge' carries smooth apple-green leaves rimmed in a thin, bright ruby-red line, a contrast that sharpens in cool weather and under strong direct sun. It stays a manageable, tidy size and lacks the cobwebbing of many alpine hybrids, making the clean green-and-red edging easy to read from a distance. Grow it in sharply drained, lean soil, since standing winter moisture is a bigger threat to this hardy succulent than freezing temperatures. Offsets form freely around each parent rosette, so a single plant fills out into a dense mat within a season or two.
sources: Chelsea Physic Garden succulent collection notes

planting.note: Press offsets into lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; German for amber, this cultivar name reflects its warm honey-bronze rosette color.

directions: 'Bernstein' takes its name from the German word for amber, describing the warm honey-bronze tone that spreads across its rosettes when grown in strong sun and lean soil. The color deepens with heat and mineral stress, giving muddier olive tones in shade or overly fertile ground. As with other hardy houseleeks, mature rosettes send up a single flowering stalk and then die, while offsets on short stolons steadily replace them. Sharp drainage matters more than winter cold for keeping this alpine succulent healthy through wet seasons.

common_name: Ohio Burgundy Hens and Chicks (Deep Wine-Red Sempervivum)

planting.note: Set offsets on the surface of lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun, where cool weather deepens the wine-burgundy color.

directions: American-bred 'Ohio Burgundy' turns a deep, saturated wine-red across nearly the whole rosette once cool fall and spring temperatures set in, fading to a duller green-burgundy in high summer heat. Full sun and lean, mineral soil sharpen the color and keep growth compact, while shade or rich soil produce looser, greener rosettes. It flowers and dies back on a single stalk like all true sempervivums, but the plant persists through its steady supply of offsets. This cultivar tolerates hot, humid summers reasonably well for a Sempervivum, making it a dependable choice for rock gardens outside the coolest climates.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh winter wind and midday summer sun.

directions: 'Compacta' grows into a denser, more rounded shrub than the wild species, with narrower leaves and a slower rate of growth that suits smaller foundation plantings and mixed shade borders. In mid-spring it carries abundant drooping clusters of small, faintly pink-tinged white flowers set off by glossy dark evergreen foliage. Grow it in consistently moist but well-drained, acidic soil rich in organic matter, and avoid drying wind and reflected summer heat, which can scorch the leaves. Established plants need little pruning beyond removing spent flower clusters and any winter-damaged twigs.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this is an unusually slow, extra-dwarf selection best sited where its small mature size will not be crowded out.

directions: 'Bisbee Dwarf' is a diminutive sport of Japanese pieris that grows only a fraction as fast as the species, forming a tight, rounded mound of small, glossy evergreen leaves over many years. Sparse clusters of small white urn-shaped flowers appear in spring, though the plant is grown chiefly for its compact form and fine texture rather than a heavy bloom display. It needs the same moist, acidic, well-drained soil and wind-sheltered partial shade as other pieris, and is well suited to trough plantings, rock gardens, and the front of small shade borders where a full-size andromeda would quickly overwhelm the space. Because new growth is slow, little to no pruning is needed to keep its neat habit.
